﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes.﴾ That is, on the day the Horn is blown into, which is the trumpet that Israfil blows into. What is meant here is the second blast, which is for the resurrection. ﴿And you will come﴾, that is, to the place of gathering, ﴿in multitudes﴾, that is, in throngs upon throngs and groups upon groups; afwaj is the plural of fawj. The accusative of ﴿the Day the Horn is blown﴾ is either as a substitute for the Day of Decision, or as an explanation of it which adds to its magnification and awesomeness, even though the decision comes after the blowing. It may also be governed by an implied verb (a'nee, "I mean"). The accusative of ﴿in multitudes﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of ta'tun. The fa' in ﴿then you will come﴾ is the fa' of explanation (fasiha), indicating an omitted element: that is, "then you will come to the place of gathering immediately after that, in multitudes."

﴿And the heaven will be opened and will become gates.﴾ It is conjoined to yunfakh, and the past tense is used to indicate the certainty of its occurrence: that is, it will be opened for the descent of the angels. ﴿And it will become gates﴾, as in His saying: ﴿And the day the heaven will be split open with clouds and the angels will be sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It is also said that the meaning of futihat is that it is cut and becomes pieces like gates. It is also said that its gates are its paths. It is also said that it will dissolve and scatter until gates appear in it. It is also said that every servant has two doors in the heaven: a door for his provision and a door for his deeds; when the Resurrection occurs, the doors will open. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿and it will become gates﴾ is that all of it becomes gates, but that is not the intended meaning; rather the intended meaning is that it becomes possessed of many gates.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read futihat with a light (unemphasized) pronunciation. The rest read it with the emphatic (shaddah) pronunciation.

﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and will become a mirage.﴾ That is, they will be moved from their places in the air and uprooted from their settings, and they will become scattered dust, so that the observer thinks they are a mirage. The meaning is that the mountains will become as nothing, just as the observer thinks the mirage is water while it is not water. It is also said that the meaning of suyyirat is that they will be uprooted from their bases.

Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass away as the clouds pass away﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Allah, glory be to Him, has described the states of the mountains in various ways, but the way to reconcile them is to say: their first state is crumbling, which is His saying: ﴿And the earth and the mountains will be lifted and crushed with one blow﴾ [al-Haqqah: 14]. Their second state is that they become like carded wool, as in His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. Their third state is that they become like dust, which is His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be pulverized to powder, and become scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6]. Their fourth state is that they will be blown away and carried by the winds, as in His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass away as the clouds pass away﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Their fifth state is that they become a mirage, that is, nothing, as in this verse.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to detail the rulings of the Decision, and said: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been an ambush.﴾ Al-Azhari said: al-mirsad is the place where the watcher watches for the enemy.

Al-Mubarrad said: mirsadan, they lie in wait for them with it; that is, it is prepared for them, and its guardians lie in wait for the disbelievers in it.

Al-Hasan said: there is an ambush at the gate; no one enters Paradise until he passes by them. Whoever comes with a pass is allowed through, and whoever does not come with a pass is detained.

Muqatil said: a prison. It is also said: a path and a passage.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: the rasid of a thing is the one who watches it. One says rasadahu yarsudahu rasdan, and al-rasd is watching, and al-marsad is the place of watching.

Al-Asma'i said: rasadtuhu arsuduhu: I watched him. The meaning of the verse is that Hell, by the decree and judgment of Allah, is a place of ambush where the guardians of the Fire lie in wait for the disbelievers to torment them therein; or it is itself watching for those who come to it from the disbelievers, just as an ambush watches for whoever passes by it and comes to them. Al-mirsad is a mif'al from the forms of intensive nouns, like al-mi'tar and al-mi'mar, so it is as if Hell's watching for the disbelievers is continuous.

Then He mentioned who it is an ambush for, saying: ﴿For the tyrants a destination.﴾ That is, a place of return to which they return. Al-ma'ab is the return; one says aba ya'ubu when he returns. The tagheen is the one who transgresses through disbelief. The phrase lil-tagheen is a qualifier of ﴿mirsadan﴾, connected to an implied element, and ma'aban is a substitute for ﴿mirsadan﴾. It is also permissible for lil-tagheen to be in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of ma'aban, placed before it because it is indefinite.

The accusative of ﴿remaining therein﴾ is a future circumstantial state (hal muqaddarah) of the pronoun hidden in al-tagheen.

The majority read ﴿lubithin﴾ with an alif. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "labithin" without an alif.

The accusative of ﴿ahqaban﴾ is adverbial of time: that is, remaining in the Fire for as long as the ahqab (ages) last, and they never end; whenever one huqb passes, another huqb comes. It is the plural of huqub with two damma, meaning an age of time, and al-ahqab are ages. The huqb with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the qaf: it is said it is eighty years. Al-Wahidi related from the commentators that it is "eighty-odd years," a year being three hundred and sixty days, and a day being a thousand years of the days of this world.

It is also said that the ahqab is a time for their drinking the boiling water and the ghassaq; when they are finished, there will be another kind of punishment for them.

Al-Suddi said: the huqb is seventy years.

Bashir ibn Ka'b said: three hundred years.

Ibn 'Umar said: forty years. It is also said: thirty thousand years.

Al-Hasan said: none of you knows what the ahqab are, but they mentioned that they are a hundred huqb, and one huqb of them is seventy thousand years, a day of them being like a thousand years.

It is also said that the verse is to be understood as applying to the sinners who will come out of the Fire. The first view that we mentioned is preferable, namely that the verse's intent is eternity, not limitation.

Al-Wahidi related from al-Hasan that he said: "By Allah, it is nothing but that when one huqb passes, another enters, then another, and so on forever."

The clause ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except boiling water and ghassaq﴾ is a resumptive sentence explaining what the previous clause contains: that they will not taste in Hell, or during the ahqab, any coolness that would benefit them from its heat, nor any drink that would benefit them from their thirst, except hamim, which is boiling water, and ghassaq, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

It may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the pronoun of the tagheen, or an attribute of the ahqab. The exception is disjunct according to those who take bard to mean sleep. It may also be conjunct, from His saying ﴿drink﴾.

Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu 'Ubayda, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: the bard mentioned in this verse is sleep, and from it is the saying of al-Kindi:

*Her cheeks grew cool upon me, so the cold kept me*
*away from her and from kissing her, the cold.*

That is, sleep.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, they will not taste therein the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep, so bard is made to include these matters.

Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: bardan means rawh (comfort) and rawahah (relief).

The majority read ghassaqan with light pronunciation. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the doubled sin. Its explanation and the explanation of hamim, and the difference of readings concerning them, have already been mentioned in Surah Sad.

﴿A fitting recompense.﴾ That is, in accordance with their deeds. Jaza' is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and wifaqan is its attribute.

Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: we recompensed them with a recompense that matched their deeds. Al-Zajjaj said: they were recompensed with a recompense that matched their deeds.

Al-Farra' said: al-wifaq is the plural of al-wafq, and al-wafq and al-muwafiq are one.

Muqatil said: the punishment matched the sin; there is no sin greater than evil, and no punishment greater than the Fire.

Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought them what would hurt them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning.﴾ That is, they did not expect the reward of a reckoning.

Al-Zajjaj said: they did not believe in the resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning. The clause is a justification for their deserving the mentioned recompense.

﴿And they denied Our signs with vehement denial.﴾ That is, they denied the Quranic verses, or they denied what is more general than them, with intense denial. Fi'ial is from the verbal nouns of the tafa''ul form.

Al-Farra' said: it is an eloquent Yemeni dialect; one says kadhdhabtu kidhdhaban and kharraqtu al-qamis kharraqan.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "and they denied Our signs with kidhdhaban" is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come as taf'il like al-takleem, as fi'al like kidhdhab, as taf'ilah like tawsiyah, and as mufa''al like "And We tore them to shreds, every shred" [Saba: 19]. The majority read kidhdhaban with doubling.

Ali ibn Abi Talib read it with light pronunciation.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the light and the doubled forms are both the verbal noun of al-mukadhabah (denial).

Ibn 'Umar read kuddhaban with a damma on the kaf and doubling, as the plural of kadhib.

Abu Hatim said: its accusative is circumstantial.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it may also (meaning in this reading) mean the one who is eloquent in lying, as you say rajulun kaddhab like your saying hassan and bakhhal.

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record.﴾ The majority read wa-kulla with the accusative by the construction of suppression: that is, "And We have enumerated everything We have enumerated."

Abu al-Simak read it with the nominative as an inceptive, and what follows is its predicate, and this clause is interposed between the cause and its effect. The accusative of kitaban is a verbal noun for ahsaynahu, since ahsaynahu has the meaning of kataba-nahu (We wrote it). It is also said it is accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, written. It is said the meaning is what We wrote in the Preserved Tablet so that the angels would know it. It is said it means what the guardian angels wrote concerning the deeds of the servants. It is also said it means knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. The first is preferable, given His saying: ﴿And everything We have enumerated in a clear record﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12].

﴿So taste, for We will not increase you except in punishment.﴾ This clause is causally linked to their disbelief and denial of the signs.

Al-Razi said: this fa' is for the recompense, indicating that the command to taste is grounded in the previously explained evil of their deeds. Among the increase in their punishment is that whenever their skins are burned, Allah replaces them with other skins, and whenever the fire subsides, Allah increases them in blaze.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿about the great news﴾ that he said: it is the Quran. This is also narrated from a group of the Successors.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying ﴿and We made a blazing lamp﴾ that he said: shining. ﴿And We sent down from the rain-clouds﴾ he said: the clouds. ﴿Water pouring forth﴾ he said: poured out.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning ﴿pouring forth﴾ that he said: poured out.

Al-Shafi'i, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying ﴿And We sent down from the rain-clouds water pouring forth﴾ that he said: Allah sends the wind, and it carries the water, and the clouds pass over it and are milked like a milch camel is milked. The pouring water descends from the sky like great drops, and the winds scatter it so that it falls in scattered form.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif related from Qatadah that he said: in the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, "And We sent down from the rain-clouds by the winds."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying ﴿And gardens of thick foliage﴾ that he said: intertwined.

Ibn Jarir also related from him concerning the verse that he said: he says: some of it has entwined with others.

Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning His saying ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and will become a mirage﴾ that he said: the mirage of the sun, which is the shimmering.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) regarding ﴿lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾ (﴿remaining therein for ages﴾) that he said: "Years."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Salim ibn Abi al-Jaʿd, who said: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib asked Hilal al-Hajari: "What do you find the ḥuqb (an extremely long, indefinite span of time) to be in the Book of Allah?" He replied: "We find it to be eighty years, each year consisting of twelve months, each month thirty days, and each day a thousand years."

Saʿid ibn Mansur and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Masʿud regarding the verse that he said: "One ḥuqb is eighty years."

al-Bazzar narrated from Abu Hurayra, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is like a thousand years of what you count."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from him (Abu Hurayra) that he said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, a day of which is like a sixth of the world."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated...

al-Suyuti said: With a weak chain, from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding ﴿lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾, he said: "The ḥuqb is a thousand months, a month is thirty days, and a year is twelve months, three hundred and sixty days, each day of which is a thousand years of what you count. So the ḥuqb is thirty thousand years."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "By Allah, whoever enters the Fire will not leave it until he remains in it for ages. The ḥuqb is some eighty years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count."

Ibn Umar said: "So let no one rely on the belief that he will leave the Fire."

Saʿid ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "One ḥuqb is eighty years."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas the same.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubada ibn al-Samit who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The ḥuqb is forty years."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Khalid ibn Maʿdan regarding His saying ﴿lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾ and His saying ﴿illā mā shāʾa rabbuka﴾ (﴿except what your Lord wills﴾), that both apply to the people of monotheism among the people of the qiblah.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Masʿud who said: "The zamharir (extreme cold) of Hell is part of their punishment, because Allah says: ﴿lā yadhūqūna fīhā bardan wa-lā sharāban﴾ (﴿they will not taste therein any coolness or drink﴾)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿lā yadhūqūna fīhā bardan wa-lā sharāban illā ḥamīman﴾ (﴿they will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except boiling water﴾), he said: "Its heat has reached its limit," and ﴿wa-ghassāqan﴾ (﴿and dark, pus-like fluid﴾): "Its heat has reached its limit. When a man brings the vessel to his mouth, the skin of his face falls off, until only bones remain, rattling."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿jazāʾan wifāqā﴾ (﴿a fitting recompense﴾) that he said: "It corresponded to their deeds."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "No verse was ever revealed concerning the people of the Fire more severe than this: ﴿fadhūqū falan nazīdakum illā ʿadhāban﴾ (﴿So taste, and We will not increase you except in punishment﴾). They will be in ever-increasing punishment from Allah forever."

This is Meccan according to all.
Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "﴿Concerning what are they asking one another?﴾ was revealed in Mecca."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿ʿamma yatasaʾalun﴾ (concerning what they question one another). Its original form is ʿan mā, and the nun was assimilated into the mīm, because the mīm shares with it the nasalization (ghunna). So said al-Zajjaj.
The alif was deleted so that the statement would be distinguished from the interrogative, and likewise fīma, mimma and the like. The meaning: "About what thing do some of them ask others?"

The majority read ʿammа (with the alif deleted) for the reason we mentioned. Ubayy, Ibn Masʿud, ʿIkrimah and ʿIsa read it with the alif retained, and from this is the saying of the poet:
"ʿalāma qāma yashtumunī la'īmun / kakhinzīrin tamarraghā fī damān"
But this is rare and is permitted only out of necessity. al-Bazzi read it with the silent hāʾ (hāʾ al-sakt) in place of the alif, and this is related from Ibn Kathir.

Al-Zajjaj said: The wording is that of a question, but the meaning is the magnification of the matter, as you say, "What thing do you want?" when you wish to exalt its importance.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent and informed them of the Oneness of Allah and resurrection after death, and recited the Qur'an to them, they began to question one another, saying: "What has Muhammad brought, and what is it that he has come with?" So Allah revealed ﴿ʿamma yatasaʾalun﴾. al-Farra said: Tasaʾul is that some of them ask others, in the manner of reciprocity; but it is also used for conversing about it even when there is no question between them.

Allah Most High said: ﴿So some of them turned to others, questioning one another﴾ [al-Saffat 50–51], and ﴿A speaker among them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ — the verse. This indicates that it means conversation. The word mā is laid down for seeking the realities of things, and this requires that what is sought be unknown. So the great matter whose true nature the intellect cannot fully encompass is treated as unknown; for this reason He, glory be to Him, used the word mā.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what they were asking about and explained it, saying: ﴿about the great news﴾. He first presented it in the form of an interrogative, vague, so that their minds would be directed to it and their understandings would attend to it; then He specified it with what conveys its magnification and exaltation, as if it were said: "About what thing are they questioning? Has He informed you of it?" Then it was said by way of answer: ﴿about the great news﴾, following the pattern of His saying: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today? To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir 16]. So the prepositional phrase is connected to the verb before it, or to what indicates it.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Most grammarians said: ʿan al-naba' al-ʿazim is connected to the apparent yatasaʾaluna, as if he said: "Why do they question one another about the great news?" It was also said that it is not connected to the mentioned verb, because that would require the entry of the interrogative particle, and the meaning would be "About the great news?" Therefore it must be connected to another implied verb of questioning. That news — that is, the Qur'an — was great because it informs of Tawhid, the confirmation of the Messenger, and the occurrence of resurrection and rising.

al-Dahhak said: It means the news of the Day of Resurrection, and Qatadah said likewise.

It has been argued that the great news is the Qur'an, from His saying: ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾, for they differed concerning the Qur'an: some said it was magic, some said it was poetry, some said it was soothsaying, and some said it was "tales of the ancients."

As for resurrection, the unbelievers at that time were in agreement in denying it.
It may be said that disagreement about resurrection in general did occur: the believers affirmed it and the disbelievers denied it, so disagreement regarding it arose from this standpoint, even if the disbelievers did not disagree among themselves about it in the sense of acceptance and acquiescence. Among what indicates that it is the Qur'an is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Say: It is a great news, from which you turn away﴾. Among what indicates that it is resurrection is that it was most often what the polytheists denied, and their feeble minds rejected it.

Moreover, among the groups of unbelievers there was disagreement about resurrection: the Christians affirmed a spiritual return, and a group of Jews affirmed a bodily return. In the Torah there is explicit mention of Paradise in the Hebrew language, by the word "Janʿīdhā" — with a fatḥa on the jīm, then a silent nūn, then a kasra on an unmarked ʿayn, then a silent unmarked yāʾ, then a marked dhāl followed by an alif.
In the Gospel, in many places, resurrection is explicitly mentioned, and that there will be bliss in it for the obedient and punishment for the disobedient. Some groups of the Arab unbelievers denied the return, as Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world: we die and we live, and we shall not be resurrected﴾ [al-Muʾminun 37]. Some of them were not firmly certain in negating it, but were doubtful about it, as Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿We think only a thought, and we are not certain﴾ [al-Jathiyah 32], and what He related of them in His saying: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will come; and if I am returned to my Lord, surely I shall have the best with Him﴾ [Fussilat 50]. Thus disagreement arose among the groups of disbelief in this manner.

It has been said that the pronoun in His saying ﴿yatasaʾalun﴾ refers to both the believers and the disbelievers, because they all were questioning about it: as for the Muslim, it increases him in certainty, readiness and insight into his religion; as for the disbeliever, it is with mockery and derision.

al-Razi said: It is possible that they were asking the Messenger, saying: "What is this that he promises us of the matter of the Hereafter?" The relative clause is in the position of a genitive qualifier of al-naba', after its description as great; so it is characterized by greatness and also by the occurrence of disagreement concerning it.

﴿Nay, they will come to know﴾ — a rebuke and a warning for them. This shows that those who differ about it are the disbelievers, and by this is refuted what was said, that the disagreement is between them and the believers, since the threat and warning are directed only at the disbelievers. It was also said: "kallā" means "truly." Then He repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿Then nay, they will come to know﴾, for emphasis and intensification of the threat.

The majority read both verbs with the yāʾ (third person). Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Ibn Dinar, and Ibn ʿAmir in one narration from him read them with the tāʾ (second person).
al-Dahhak read the first with tāʾ and the second with yāʾ.

al-Dahhak also said: ﴿Nay, they will come to know﴾ means the disbelievers, the outcome of their denial; ﴿then nay, they will come to know﴾ means the believers, the outcome of their affirmation. It was also said the reverse. It was said that it is one threat after another threat. It was said that the meaning of ﴿Nay, they will come to know﴾ is at the moment of extraction (al-nazʿ), and ﴿then nay, they will come to know﴾ is at the resurrection.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the wonder of His creation and the greatness of His power, so that they might know His Oneness and believe in what His Messenger brought, saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the wonder of His creation and the greatness of His power, so that they might know His Oneness and believe in what His Messenger brought, saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place, and the mountains as pegs?﴾ That is, Our power over these mentioned matters is greater than Our power over restoration by resurrection. al-Mihad is the spread and the bedding, as in His saying: ﴿Who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 22]. The majority read mihadan; Mujahid, ʿIsa and some of the Kufans read "mahdan," and the meaning is that it is like a cradle for the infant, which is what is prepared for him so that he sleeps upon it.

And awtad is the plural of watad: that is, We made the mountains pegs for the earth, so that it may be stable and not move, just as tents are fixed with pegs. In this is evidence that the questioning occurring among them is about the matter of resurrection, not about the Qur'an nor about the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ as has been said; for this argument is only suitable to be used as proof for resurrection.

﴿And We created you in pairs﴾ is coordinated with the negated present verb and falls under its ruling, so it is in the sense of "As for: We created you." By "pairs" here is meant kinds: that is, males and females. It was said that "pairs" means colors. It was said that every pair among created things is included in this, whether ugly or beautiful, tall or short.

﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾: that is, a repose for your bodies.

al-Zajjaj said: subat is that one ceases from movement while the spirit remains in his body: that is, We made your sleep a rest for you.
Ibn al-Anbari said: We made your sleep a cessation of your activities, for the root of sabt is cutting. It was also said its root is stretching out: one says "sabatat al-mar'ah sha'rahā" when she loosens and releases it, and "rajul masbūt al-khalq" means one who is stretched out; and when a man wishes to rest he stretches himself out, so sleep is called subat. It was also said the meaning is: We made your sleep a death, and sleep is one of the two deaths; the one who is in subat resembles the dead, but the spirit has not left him. From this is the saying of the poet:
"wa-matwiyyat al-aqrāb ammā nahāruhā / fasabatun wa-ammā laylahā fadhamīlu"
From this is His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died in their sleep﴾ [al-Zumar 42], and His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you in death by night﴾ [al-Anʿam 60].

﴿And We made the night a garment﴾: that is, We clothe you with its darkness and cover you with it as a garment covers you.
Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said: that is, a dwelling for you. It was said that what is meant is what one covers oneself with during sleep, such as a blanket and the like; but this is far-fetched, because the making was applied to the night, not to what the sleeper covers himself with during his sleep.

﴿And We made the day a means of livelihood﴾: that is, a time of livelihood. Al-maʿash is living, and everything by which one lives is maʿash. The meaning is that Allah made the day bright for them so that they might strive in what sustains their livelihood and what Allah has apportioned to them of provision.

﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾: He means seven heavens, strong in creation and firm in construction; for this reason He described them with strength, and the thickness of each one is a five-hundred-year journey, as has been reported.

﴿And We made a blazing lamp﴾: what is meant is the sun. Here jaʿala means khalaqa (created), and likewise His saying: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾ and what follows it (p-1575), because these verbs take two objects, so they must be construed with a verb that takes both objects, such as "created" or "made" and the like.
It was also said that jaʿl here means origination and innovation in all these places, and what is meant is creative origination, in the sense of determination and arrangement.

al-Zajjaj said: al-wahhaj is the blazing one, which is what glows; one says "wahajat al-nār tahij wahjan wa-wahajānan."
Muqatil said: He placed in it a hot light; and al-wahaj combines light and heat.

﴿And We sent down from the pressing clouds water pouring abundantly﴾: al-muʿsirat are the clouds that are pressed with water and have not yet rained, like a woman in labor whose time of menstruation is near; so said Sufyan, al-Rabi', Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Dahhak.
Mujahid, Muqatil, Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: they are the winds, and winds are called muʿsirat; one says "a'ṣarat al-rīḥ taʿṣiru iʿṣāran" when it raises dust.
al-Azhari said: they are the winds with whirlwinds, because the winds draw forth rain.
al-Farra said: al-muʿsirat are the clouds from which rain drips.
al-Nahhas said: These sayings are sound: the wind that brings rain is called muʿsirat, and the winds impregnate the clouds so that rain comes.
It is permissible that these sayings are one saying, and the meaning is: "And We sent down from the possessors of muʿsirat water pouring abundantly."
Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: al-muʿsirat are the clouds that squeeze out rain; and "ʿuṣira al-qawm" means they were rained upon.
al-Mubarrad said: one says "saḥāb muʿsir," meaning one that holds water and squeezes out some of it little by little.
Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: al-muʿsirat are the heavens. And al-thajjaj is that which pours down in abundance in a continuous manner; one says "thajja al-mā'" meaning the water flowed abundantly, and "thajjahu" meaning he made it flow.
al-Zajjaj said: al-thajjaj is the one who pours continuously.
Ibn Zayd said: thajjājan means abundant.

﴿So that We may bring forth thereby grain and plants﴾: that is, so that We may bring forth by that water grain that is eaten as food, like wheat, barley and the like; and al-nabat is what the animals eat of grass and all other plants.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 78, verse 1–30 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And gardens of thick foliage.﴾ That is, orchards whose trees intertwine with one another because of the branching of their boughs. The word alfaf has no singular, like awza' and akhyaf. It is also said that its singular is laff, with the lam either kasra or damma, as mentioned by al-Kisa'i.

Abu 'Ubayda said: its singular is lafif, like sharif and ashraf. It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that it is a plural of a plural: one says jannah lafa' (a garden of thick foliage) and nabt laff (dense vegetation), the plural being laff with the lam damma, like humr. This plural is then pluralized again as alfaf. It is also said that it is the plural of multaffah, with the extra letters removed.

Al-Farra' said: the jannah is that which contains palm trees, and the firdaws is that which contains vines.

﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time.﴾ That is, a time, a gathering and an appointment for the first and the last, when they will reach what they were promised of reward and punishment. It was named the Day of Decision because Allah decides among His creation on it. This is the beginning of the explanation of what they question about, namely the resurrection. It is also said that the meaning of mi'aqat is that it is a limit by which the world is timed and at which it ends. It is also said that it is a limit for creatures at which they arrive.

﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes.﴾ That is, on the day the Horn is blown into, which is the trumpet that Israfil blows into. What is meant here is the second blast, which is for the resurrection. ﴿And you will come﴾, that is, to the place of gathering, ﴿in multitudes﴾, that is, in throngs upon throngs and groups upon groups; afwaj is the plural of fawj. The accusative of ﴿the Day the Horn is blown﴾ is either as a substitute for the Day of Decision, or as an explanation of it which adds to its magnification and awesomeness, even though the decision comes after the blowing. It may also be governed by an implied verb (a'nee, "I mean"). The accusative of ﴿in multitudes﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of ta'tun. The fa' in ﴿then you will come﴾ is the fa' of explanation (fasiha), indicating an omitted element: that is, "then you will come to the place of gathering immediately after that, in multitudes."

﴿And the heaven will be opened and will become gates.﴾ It is conjoined to yunfakh, and the past tense is used to indicate the certainty of its occurrence: that is, it will be opened for the descent of the angels. ﴿And it will become gates﴾, as in His saying: ﴿And the day the heaven will be split open with clouds and the angels will be sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It is also said that the meaning of futihat is that it is cut and becomes pieces like gates. It is also said that its gates are its paths. It is also said that it will dissolve and scatter until gates appear in it. It is also said that every servant has two doors in the heaven: a door for his provision and a door for his deeds; when the Resurrection occurs, the doors will open. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿and it will become gates﴾ is that all of it becomes gates, but that is not the intended meaning; rather the intended meaning is that it becomes possessed of many gates.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read futihat with a light (unemphasized) pronunciation. The rest read it with the emphatic (shaddah) pronunciation.

﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and will become a mirage.﴾ That is, they will be moved from their places in the air and uprooted from their settings, and they will become scattered dust, so that the observer thinks they are a mirage. The meaning is that the mountains will become as nothing, just as the observer thinks the mirage is water while it is not water. It is also said that the meaning of suyyirat is that they will be uprooted from their bases.

Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass away as the clouds pass away﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Allah, glory be to Him, has described the states of the mountains in various ways, but the way to reconcile them is to say: their first state is crumbling, which is His saying: ﴿And the earth and the mountains will be lifted and crushed with one blow﴾ [al-Haqqah: 14]. Their second state is that they become like carded wool, as in His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. Their third state is that they become like dust, which is His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be pulverized to powder, and become scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6]. Their fourth state is that they will be blown away and carried by the winds, as in His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass away as the clouds pass away﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Their fifth state is that they become a mirage, that is, nothing, as in this verse.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to detail the rulings of the Decision, and said: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been an ambush.﴾ Al-Azhari said: al-mirsad is the place where the watcher watches for the enemy.

Al-Mubarrad said: mirsadan, they lie in wait for them with it; that is, it is prepared for them, and its guardians lie in wait for the disbelievers in it.

Al-Hasan said: there is an ambush at the gate; no one enters Paradise until he passes by them. Whoever comes with a pass is allowed through, and whoever does not come with a pass is detained.

Muqatil said: a prison. It is also said: a path and a passage.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: the rasid of a thing is the one who watches it. One says rasadahu yarsudahu rasdan, and al-rasd is watching, and al-marsad is the place of watching.

Al-Asma'i said: rasadtuhu arsuduhu: I watched him. The meaning of the verse is that Hell, by the decree and judgment of Allah, is a place of ambush where the guardians of the Fire lie in wait for the disbelievers to torment them therein; or it is itself watching for those who come to it from the disbelievers, just as an ambush watches for whoever passes by it and comes to them. Al-mirsad is a mif'al from the forms of intensive nouns, like al-mi'tar and al-mi'mar, so it is as if Hell's watching for the disbelievers is continuous.

Then He mentioned who it is an ambush for, saying: ﴿For the tyrants a destination.﴾ That is, a place of return to which they return. Al-ma'ab is the return; one says aba ya'ubu when he returns. The tagheen is the one who transgresses through disbelief. The phrase lil-tagheen is a qualifier of ﴿mirsadan﴾, connected to an implied element, and ma'aban is a substitute for ﴿mirsadan﴾. It is also permissible for lil-tagheen to be in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of ma'aban, placed before it because it is indefinite.

The accusative of ﴿remaining therein﴾ is a future circumstantial state (hal muqaddarah) of the pronoun hidden in al-tagheen.

The majority read ﴿lubithin﴾ with an alif. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "labithin" without an alif.

The accusative of ﴿ahqaban﴾ is adverbial of time: that is, remaining in the Fire for as long as the ahqab (ages) last, and they never end; whenever one huqb passes, another huqb comes. It is the plural of huqub with two damma, meaning an age of time, and al-ahqab are ages. The huqb with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the qaf: it is said it is eighty years. Al-Wahidi related from the commentators that it is "eighty-odd years," a year being three hundred and sixty days, and a day being a thousand years of the days of this world.

It is also said that the ahqab is a time for their drinking the boiling water and the ghassaq; when they are finished, there will be another kind of punishment for them.

Al-Suddi said: the huqb is seventy years.

Bashir ibn Ka'b said: three hundred years.

Ibn 'Umar said: forty years. It is also said: thirty thousand years.

Al-Hasan said: none of you knows what the ahqab are, but they mentioned that they are a hundred huqb, and one huqb of them is seventy thousand years, a day of them being like a thousand years.

It is also said that the verse is to be understood as applying to the sinners who will come out of the Fire. The first view that we mentioned is preferable, namely that the verse's intent is eternity, not limitation.

Al-Wahidi related from al-Hasan that he said: "By Allah, it is nothing but that when one huqb passes, another enters, then another, and so on forever."

The clause ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except boiling water and ghassaq﴾ is a resumptive sentence explaining what the previous clause contains: that they will not taste in Hell, or during the ahqab, any coolness that would benefit them from its heat, nor any drink that would benefit them from their thirst, except hamim, which is boiling water, and ghassaq, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

It may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the pronoun of the tagheen, or an attribute of the ahqab. The exception is disjunct according to those who take bard to mean sleep. It may also be conjunct, from His saying ﴿drink﴾.

Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu 'Ubayda, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: the bard mentioned in this verse is sleep, and from it is the saying of al-Kindi:

*Her cheeks grew cool upon me, so the cold kept me*
*away from her and from kissing her, the cold.*

That is, sleep.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, they will not taste therein the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep, so bard is made to include these matters.

Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: bardan means rawh (comfort) and rawahah (relief).

The majority read ghassaqan with light pronunciation. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the doubled sin. Its explanation and the explanation of hamim, and the difference of readings concerning them, have already been mentioned in Surah Sad.

﴿A fitting recompense.﴾ That is, in accordance with their deeds. Jaza' is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and wifaqan is its attribute.

Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: we recompensed them with a recompense that matched their deeds. Al-Zajjaj said: they were recompensed with a recompense that matched their deeds.

Al-Farra' said: al-wifaq is the plural of al-wafq, and al-wafq and al-muwafiq are one.

Muqatil said: the punishment matched the sin; there is no sin greater than evil, and no punishment greater than the Fire.

Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought them what would hurt them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning.﴾ That is, they did not expect the reward of a reckoning.

Al-Zajjaj said: they did not believe in the resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning. The clause is a justification for their deserving the mentioned recompense.

﴿And they denied Our signs with vehement denial.﴾ That is, they denied the Quranic verses, or they denied what is more general than them, with intense denial. Fi'ial is from the verbal nouns of the tafa''ul form.

Al-Farra' said: it is an eloquent Yemeni dialect; one says kadhdhabtu kidhdhaban and kharraqtu al-qamis kharraqan.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "and they denied Our signs with kidhdhaban" is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come as taf'il like al-takleem, as fi'al like kidhdhab, as taf'ilah like tawsiyah, and as mufa''al like "And We tore them to shreds, every shred" [Saba: 19]. The majority read kidhdhaban with doubling.

Ali ibn Abi Talib read it with light pronunciation.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the light and the doubled forms are both the verbal noun of al-mukadhabah (denial).

Ibn 'Umar read kuddhaban with a damma on the kaf and doubling, as the plural of kadhib.

Abu Hatim said: its accusative is circumstantial.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it may also (meaning in this reading) mean the one who is eloquent in lying, as you say rajulun kaddhab like your saying hassan and bakhhal.

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record.﴾ The majority read wa-kulla with the accusative by the construction of suppression: that is, "And We have enumerated everything We have enumerated."

Abu al-Simak read it with the nominative as an inceptive, and what follows is its predicate, and this clause is interposed between the cause and its effect. The accusative of kitaban is a verbal noun for ahsaynahu, since ahsaynahu has the meaning of kataba-nahu (We wrote it). It is also said it is accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, written. It is said the meaning is what We wrote in the Preserved Tablet so that the angels would know it. It is said it means what the guardian angels wrote concerning the deeds of the servants. It is also said it means knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. The first is preferable, given His saying: ﴿And everything We have enumerated in a clear record﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12].

﴿So taste, for We will not increase you except in punishment.﴾ This clause is causally linked to their disbelief and denial of the signs.

Al-Razi said: this fa' is for the recompense, indicating that the command to taste is grounded in the previously explained evil of their deeds. Among the increase in their punishment is that whenever their skins are burned, Allah replaces them with other skins, and whenever the fire subsides, Allah increases them in blaze.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿about the great news﴾ that he said: it is the Quran. This is also narrated from a group of the Successors.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying ﴿and We made a blazing lamp﴾ that he said: shining. ﴿And We sent down from the rain-clouds﴾ he said: the clouds. ﴿Water pouring forth﴾ he said: poured out.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning ﴿pouring forth﴾ that he said: poured out.

Al-Shafi'i, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying ﴿And We sent down from the rain-clouds water pouring forth﴾ that he said: Allah sends the wind, and it carries the water, and the clouds pass over it and are milked like a milch camel is milked. The pouring water descends from the sky like great drops, and the winds scatter it so that it falls in scattered form.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif related from Qatadah that he said: in the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, "And We sent down from the rain-clouds by the winds."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying ﴿And gardens of thick foliage﴾ that he said: intertwined.

Ibn Jarir also related from him concerning the verse that he said: he says: some of it has entwined with others.

Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning His saying ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and will become a mirage﴾ that he said: the mirage of the sun, which is the shimmering.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) regarding ﴿lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾ (﴿remaining therein for ages﴾) that he said: "Years."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Salim ibn Abi al-Jaʿd, who said: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib asked Hilal al-Hajari: "What do you find the ḥuqb (an extremely long, indefinite span of time) to be in the Book of Allah?" He replied: "We find it to be eighty years, each year consisting of twelve months, each month thirty days, and each day a thousand years."

Saʿid ibn Mansur and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Masʿud regarding the verse that he said: "One ḥuqb is eighty years."

al-Bazzar narrated from Abu Hurayra, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is like a thousand years of what you count."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from him (Abu Hurayra) that he said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, a day of which is like a sixth of the world."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated...

al-Suyuti said: With a weak chain, from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding ﴿lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾, he said: "The ḥuqb is a thousand months, a month is thirty days, and a year is twelve months, three hundred and sixty days, each day of which is a thousand years of what you count. So the ḥuqb is thirty thousand years."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "By Allah, whoever enters the Fire will not leave it until he remains in it for ages. The ḥuqb is some eighty years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count."

Ibn Umar said: "So let no one rely on the belief that he will leave the Fire."

Saʿid ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "One ḥuqb is eighty years."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas the same.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ubada ibn al-Samit who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The ḥuqb is forty years."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Khalid ibn Maʿdan regarding His saying ﴿lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾ and His saying ﴿illā mā shāʾa rabbuka﴾ (﴿except what your Lord wills﴾), that both apply to the people of monotheism among the people of the qiblah.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Masʿud who said: "The zamharir (extreme cold) of Hell is part of their punishment, because Allah says: ﴿lā yadhūqūna fīhā bardan wa-lā sharāban﴾ (﴿they will not taste therein any coolness or drink﴾)."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿lā yadhūqūna fīhā bardan wa-lā sharāban illā ḥamīman﴾ (﴿they will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except boiling water﴾), he said: "Its heat has reached its limit," and ﴿wa-ghassāqan﴾ (﴿and dark, pus-like fluid﴾): "Its heat has reached its limit. When a man brings the vessel to his mouth, the skin of his face falls off, until only bones remain, rattling."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿jazāʾan wifāqā﴾ (﴿a fitting recompense﴾) that he said: "It corresponded to their deeds."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr who said: "No verse was ever revealed concerning the people of the Fire more severe than this: ﴿fadhūqū falan nazīdakum illā ʿadhāban﴾ (﴿So taste, and We will not increase you except in punishment﴾). They will be in ever-increasing punishment from Allah forever."

This is Meccan according to all.
Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "﴿Concerning what are they asking one another?﴾ was revealed in Mecca."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿ʿamma yatasaʾalun﴾ (concerning what they question one another). Its original form is ʿan mā, and the nun was assimilated into the mīm, because the mīm shares with it the nasalization (ghunna). So said al-Zajjaj.
The alif was deleted so that the statement would be distinguished from the interrogative, and likewise fīma, mimma and the like. The meaning: "About what thing do some of them ask others?"

The majority read ʿammа (with the alif deleted) for the reason we mentioned. Ubayy, Ibn Masʿud, ʿIkrimah and ʿIsa read it with the alif retained, and from this is the saying of the poet:
"ʿalāma qāma yashtumunī la'īmun / kakhinzīrin tamarraghā fī damān"
But this is rare and is permitted only out of necessity. al-Bazzi read it with the silent hāʾ (hāʾ al-sakt) in place of the alif, and this is related from Ibn Kathir.

Al-Zajjaj said: The wording is that of a question, but the meaning is the magnification of the matter, as you say, "What thing do you want?" when you wish to exalt its importance.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sent and informed them of the Oneness of Allah and resurrection after death, and recited the Qur'an to them, they began to question one another, saying: "What has Muhammad brought, and what is it that he has come with?" So Allah revealed ﴿ʿamma yatasaʾalun﴾. al-Farra said: Tasaʾul is that some of them ask others, in the manner of reciprocity; but it is also used for conversing about it even when there is no question between them.

Allah Most High said: ﴿So some of them turned to others, questioning one another﴾ [al-Saffat 50–51], and ﴿A speaker among them said: Indeed I had a companion﴾ — the verse. This indicates that it means conversation. The word mā is laid down for seeking the realities of things, and this requires that what is sought be unknown. So the great matter whose true nature the intellect cannot fully encompass is treated as unknown; for this reason He, glory be to Him, used the word mā.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned what they were asking about and explained it, saying: ﴿about the great news﴾. He first presented it in the form of an interrogative, vague, so that their minds would be directed to it and their understandings would attend to it; then He specified it with what conveys its magnification and exaltation, as if it were said: "About what thing are they questioning? Has He informed you of it?" Then it was said by way of answer: ﴿about the great news﴾, following the pattern of His saying: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today? To Allah, the One, the Subduer﴾ [Ghafir 16]. So the prepositional phrase is connected to the verb before it, or to what indicates it.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: Most grammarians said: ʿan al-naba' al-ʿazim is connected to the apparent yatasaʾaluna, as if he said: "Why do they question one another about the great news?" It was also said that it is not connected to the mentioned verb, because that would require the entry of the interrogative particle, and the meaning would be "About the great news?" Therefore it must be connected to another implied verb of questioning. That news — that is, the Qur'an — was great because it informs of Tawhid, the confirmation of the Messenger, and the occurrence of resurrection and rising.

al-Dahhak said: It means the news of the Day of Resurrection, and Qatadah said likewise.

It has been argued that the great news is the Qur'an, from His saying: ﴿about which they are in disagreement﴾, for they differed concerning the Qur'an: some said it was magic, some said it was poetry, some said it was soothsaying, and some said it was "tales of the ancients."

As for resurrection, the unbelievers at that time were in agreement in denying it.
It may be said that disagreement about resurrection in general did occur: the believers affirmed it and the disbelievers denied it, so disagreement regarding it arose from this standpoint, even if the disbelievers did not disagree among themselves about it in the sense of acceptance and acquiescence. Among what indicates that it is the Qur'an is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿Say: It is a great news, from which you turn away﴾. Among what indicates that it is resurrection is that it was most often what the polytheists denied, and their feeble minds rejected it.

Moreover, among the groups of unbelievers there was disagreement about resurrection: the Christians affirmed a spiritual return, and a group of Jews affirmed a bodily return. In the Torah there is explicit mention of Paradise in the Hebrew language, by the word "Janʿīdhā" — with a fatḥa on the jīm, then a silent nūn, then a kasra on an unmarked ʿayn, then a silent unmarked yāʾ, then a marked dhāl followed by an alif.
In the Gospel, in many places, resurrection is explicitly mentioned, and that there will be bliss in it for the obedient and punishment for the disobedient. Some groups of the Arab unbelievers denied the return, as Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿There is nothing but our life of this world: we die and we live, and we shall not be resurrected﴾ [al-Muʾminun 37]. Some of them were not firmly certain in negating it, but were doubtful about it, as Allah related of them in His saying: ﴿We think only a thought, and we are not certain﴾ [al-Jathiyah 32], and what He related of them in His saying: ﴿And I do not think the Hour will come; and if I am returned to my Lord, surely I shall have the best with Him﴾ [Fussilat 50]. Thus disagreement arose among the groups of disbelief in this manner.

It has been said that the pronoun in His saying ﴿yatasaʾalun﴾ refers to both the believers and the disbelievers, because they all were questioning about it: as for the Muslim, it increases him in certainty, readiness and insight into his religion; as for the disbeliever, it is with mockery and derision.

al-Razi said: It is possible that they were asking the Messenger, saying: "What is this that he promises us of the matter of the Hereafter?" The relative clause is in the position of a genitive qualifier of al-naba', after its description as great; so it is characterized by greatness and also by the occurrence of disagreement concerning it.

﴿Nay, they will come to know﴾ — a rebuke and a warning for them. This shows that those who differ about it are the disbelievers, and by this is refuted what was said, that the disagreement is between them and the believers, since the threat and warning are directed only at the disbelievers. It was also said: "kallā" means "truly." Then He repeated the rebuke and warning, saying: ﴿Then nay, they will come to know﴾, for emphasis and intensification of the threat.

The majority read both verbs with the yāʾ (third person). Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Ibn Dinar, and Ibn ʿAmir in one narration from him read them with the tāʾ (second person).
al-Dahhak read the first with tāʾ and the second with yāʾ.

al-Dahhak also said: ﴿Nay, they will come to know﴾ means the disbelievers, the outcome of their denial; ﴿then nay, they will come to know﴾ means the believers, the outcome of their affirmation. It was also said the reverse. It was said that it is one threat after another threat. It was said that the meaning of ﴿Nay, they will come to know﴾ is at the moment of extraction (al-nazʿ), and ﴿then nay, they will come to know﴾ is at the resurrection.

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the wonder of His creation and the greatness of His power, so that they might know His Oneness and believe in what His Messenger brought, saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place?﴾

Then He, glory be to Him, mentioned the wonder of His creation and the greatness of His power, so that they might know His Oneness and believe in what His Messenger brought, saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a resting-place, and the mountains as pegs?﴾ That is, Our power over these mentioned matters is greater than Our power over restoration by resurrection. al-Mihad is the spread and the bedding, as in His saying: ﴿Who made the earth a bed for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 22]. The majority read mihadan; Mujahid, ʿIsa and some of the Kufans read "mahdan," and the meaning is that it is like a cradle for the infant, which is what is prepared for him so that he sleeps upon it.

And awtad is the plural of watad: that is, We made the mountains pegs for the earth, so that it may be stable and not move, just as tents are fixed with pegs. In this is evidence that the questioning occurring among them is about the matter of resurrection, not about the Qur'an nor about the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ as has been said; for this argument is only suitable to be used as proof for resurrection.

﴿And We created you in pairs﴾ is coordinated with the negated present verb and falls under its ruling, so it is in the sense of "As for: We created you." By "pairs" here is meant kinds: that is, males and females. It was said that "pairs" means colors. It was said that every pair among created things is included in this, whether ugly or beautiful, tall or short.

﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾: that is, a repose for your bodies.

al-Zajjaj said: subat is that one ceases from movement while the spirit remains in his body: that is, We made your sleep a rest for you.
Ibn al-Anbari said: We made your sleep a cessation of your activities, for the root of sabt is cutting. It was also said its root is stretching out: one says "sabatat al-mar'ah sha'rahā" when she loosens and releases it, and "rajul masbūt al-khalq" means one who is stretched out; and when a man wishes to rest he stretches himself out, so sleep is called subat. It was also said the meaning is: We made your sleep a death, and sleep is one of the two deaths; the one who is in subat resembles the dead, but the spirit has not left him. From this is the saying of the poet:
"wa-matwiyyat al-aqrāb ammā nahāruhā / fasabatun wa-ammā laylahā fadhamīlu"
From this is His saying: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that have not died in their sleep﴾ [al-Zumar 42], and His saying: ﴿It is He who takes you in death by night﴾ [al-Anʿam 60].

﴿And We made the night a garment﴾: that is, We clothe you with its darkness and cover you with it as a garment covers you.
Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi said: that is, a dwelling for you. It was said that what is meant is what one covers oneself with during sleep, such as a blanket and the like; but this is far-fetched, because the making was applied to the night, not to what the sleeper covers himself with during his sleep.

﴿And We made the day a means of livelihood﴾: that is, a time of livelihood. Al-maʿash is living, and everything by which one lives is maʿash. The meaning is that Allah made the day bright for them so that they might strive in what sustains their livelihood and what Allah has apportioned to them of provision.

﴿And We built above you seven strong ones﴾: He means seven heavens, strong in creation and firm in construction; for this reason He described them with strength, and the thickness of each one is a five-hundred-year journey, as has been reported.

﴿And We made a blazing lamp﴾: what is meant is the sun. Here jaʿala means khalaqa (created), and likewise His saying: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾ and what follows it (p-1575), because these verbs take two objects, so they must be construed with a verb that takes both objects, such as "created" or "made" and the like.
It was also said that jaʿl here means origination and innovation in all these places, and what is meant is creative origination, in the sense of determination and arrangement.

al-Zajjaj said: al-wahhaj is the blazing one, which is what glows; one says "wahajat al-nār tahij wahjan wa-wahajānan."
Muqatil said: He placed in it a hot light; and al-wahaj combines light and heat.

﴿And We sent down from the pressing clouds water pouring abundantly﴾: al-muʿsirat are the clouds that are pressed with water and have not yet rained, like a woman in labor whose time of menstruation is near; so said Sufyan, al-Rabi', Abu al-ʿAliyah and al-Dahhak.
Mujahid, Muqatil, Qatadah and al-Kalbi said: they are the winds, and winds are called muʿsirat; one says "a'ṣarat al-rīḥ taʿṣiru iʿṣāran" when it raises dust.
al-Azhari said: they are the winds with whirlwinds, because the winds draw forth rain.
al-Farra said: al-muʿsirat are the clouds from which rain drips.
al-Nahhas said: These sayings are sound: the wind that brings rain is called muʿsirat, and the winds impregnate the clouds so that rain comes.
It is permissible that these sayings are one saying, and the meaning is: "And We sent down from the possessors of muʿsirat water pouring abundantly."
Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: al-muʿsirat are the clouds that squeeze out rain; and "ʿuṣira al-qawm" means they were rained upon.
al-Mubarrad said: one says "saḥāb muʿsir," meaning one that holds water and squeezes out some of it little by little.
Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, Zayd ibn Aslam and Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: al-muʿsirat are the heavens. And al-thajjaj is that which pours down in abundance in a continuous manner; one says "thajja al-mā'" meaning the water flowed abundantly, and "thajjahu" meaning he made it flow.
al-Zajjaj said: al-thajjaj is the one who pours continuously.
Ibn Zayd said: thajjājan means abundant.

﴿So that We may bring forth thereby grain and plants﴾: that is, so that We may bring forth by that water grain that is eaten as food, like wheat, barley and the like; and al-nabat is what the animals eat of grass and all other plants.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 78, verse 1–30 (part 2 of 3):

﴿And gardens of thick foliage.﴾ That is, orchards whose trees intertwine with one another because of the branching of their boughs. The word alfaf has no singular, like awza' and akhyaf. It is also said that its singular is laff, with the lam either kasra or damma, as mentioned by al-Kisa'i.

Abu 'Ubayda said: its singular is lafif, like sharif and ashraf. It is narrated from al-Kisa'i that it is a plural of a plural: one says jannah lafa' (a garden of thick foliage) and nabt laff (dense vegetation), the plural being laff with the lam damma, like humr. This plural is then pluralized again as alfaf. It is also said that it is the plural of multaffah, with the extra letters removed.

Al-Farra' said: the jannah is that which contains palm trees, and the firdaws is that which contains vines.

﴿Indeed, the Day of Decision is an appointed time.﴾ That is, a time, a gathering and an appointment for the first and the last, when they will reach what they were promised of reward and punishment. It was named the Day of Decision because Allah decides among His creation on it. This is the beginning of the explanation of what they question about, namely the resurrection. It is also said that the meaning of mi'aqat is that it is a limit by which the world is timed and at which it ends. It is also said that it is a limit for creatures at which they arrive.

﴿The Day the Horn is blown, and you will come forth in multitudes.﴾ That is, on the day the Horn is blown into, which is the trumpet that Israfil blows into. What is meant here is the second blast, which is for the resurrection. ﴿And you will come﴾, that is, to the place of gathering, ﴿in multitudes﴾, that is, in throngs upon throngs and groups upon groups; afwaj is the plural of fawj. The accusative of ﴿the Day the Horn is blown﴾ is either as a substitute for the Day of Decision, or as an explanation of it which adds to its magnification and awesomeness, even though the decision comes after the blowing. It may also be governed by an implied verb (a'nee, "I mean"). The accusative of ﴿in multitudes﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal) of the subject of ta'tun. The fa' in ﴿then you will come﴾ is the fa' of explanation (fasiha), indicating an omitted element: that is, "then you will come to the place of gathering immediately after that, in multitudes."

﴿And the heaven will be opened and will become gates.﴾ It is conjoined to yunfakh, and the past tense is used to indicate the certainty of its occurrence: that is, it will be opened for the descent of the angels. ﴿And it will become gates﴾, as in His saying: ﴿And the day the heaven will be split open with clouds and the angels will be sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]. It is also said that the meaning of futihat is that it is cut and becomes pieces like gates. It is also said that its gates are its paths. It is also said that it will dissolve and scatter until gates appear in it. It is also said that every servant has two doors in the heaven: a door for his provision and a door for his deeds; when the Resurrection occurs, the doors will open. The apparent sense of His saying ﴿and it will become gates﴾ is that all of it becomes gates, but that is not the intended meaning; rather the intended meaning is that it becomes possessed of many gates.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read futihat with a light (unemphasized) pronunciation. The rest read it with the emphatic (shaddah) pronunciation.

﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and will become a mirage.﴾ That is, they will be moved from their places in the air and uprooted from their settings, and they will become scattered dust, so that the observer thinks they are a mirage. The meaning is that the mountains will become as nothing, just as the observer thinks the mirage is water while it is not water. It is also said that the meaning of suyyirat is that they will be uprooted from their bases.

Similar to this is His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass away as the clouds pass away﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Allah, glory be to Him, has described the states of the mountains in various ways, but the way to reconcile them is to say: their first state is crumbling, which is His saying: ﴿And the earth and the mountains will be lifted and crushed with one blow﴾ [al-Haqqah: 14]. Their second state is that they become like carded wool, as in His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be like fluffed-up wool﴾ [al-Qari'ah: 5]. Their third state is that they become like dust, which is His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be pulverized to powder, and become scattered dust﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 5-6]. Their fourth state is that they will be blown away and carried by the winds, as in His saying: ﴿And you see the mountains, thinking them solid, while they pass away as the clouds pass away﴾ [al-Naml: 88]. Their fifth state is that they become a mirage, that is, nothing, as in this verse.

Then He, glory be to Him, began to detail the rulings of the Decision, and said: ﴿Indeed, Hell has been an ambush.﴾ Al-Azhari said: al-mirsad is the place where the watcher watches for the enemy.

Al-Mubarrad said: mirsadan, they lie in wait for them with it; that is, it is prepared for them, and its guardians lie in wait for the disbelievers in it.

Al-Hasan said: there is an ambush at the gate; no one enters Paradise until he passes by them. Whoever comes with a pass is allowed through, and whoever does not come with a pass is detained.

Muqatil said: a prison. It is also said: a path and a passage.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: the rasid of a thing is the one who watches it. One says rasadahu yarsudahu rasdan, and al-rasd is watching, and al-marsad is the place of watching.

Al-Asma'i said: rasadtuhu arsuduhu: I watched him. The meaning of the verse is that Hell, by the decree and judgment of Allah, is a place of ambush where the guardians of the Fire lie in wait for the disbelievers to torment them therein; or it is itself watching for those who come to it from the disbelievers, just as an ambush watches for whoever passes by it and comes to them. Al-mirsad is a mif'al from the forms of intensive nouns, like al-mi'tar and al-mi'mar, so it is as if Hell's watching for the disbelievers is continuous.

Then He mentioned who it is an ambush for, saying: ﴿For the tyrants a destination.﴾ That is, a place of return to which they return. Al-ma'ab is the return; one says aba ya'ubu when he returns. The tagheen is the one who transgresses through disbelief. The phrase lil-tagheen is a qualifier of ﴿mirsadan﴾, connected to an implied element, and ma'aban is a substitute for ﴿mirsadan﴾. It is also permissible for lil-tagheen to be in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of ma'aban, placed before it because it is indefinite.

The accusative of ﴿remaining therein﴾ is a future circumstantial state (hal muqaddarah) of the pronoun hidden in al-tagheen.

The majority read ﴿lubithin﴾ with an alif. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "labithin" without an alif.

The accusative of ﴿ahqaban﴾ is adverbial of time: that is, remaining in the Fire for as long as the ahqab (ages) last, and they never end; whenever one huqb passes, another huqb comes. It is the plural of huqub with two damma, meaning an age of time, and al-ahqab are ages. The huqb with a damma on the ha' and a sukun on the qaf: it is said it is eighty years. Al-Wahidi related from the commentators that it is "eighty-odd years," a year being three hundred and sixty days, and a day being a thousand years of the days of this world.

It is also said that the ahqab is a time for their drinking the boiling water and the ghassaq; when they are finished, there will be another kind of punishment for them.

Al-Suddi said: the huqb is seventy years.

Bashir ibn Ka'b said: three hundred years.

Ibn 'Umar said: forty years. It is also said: thirty thousand years.

Al-Hasan said: none of you knows what the ahqab are, but they mentioned that they are a hundred huqb, and one huqb of them is seventy thousand years, a day of them being like a thousand years.

It is also said that the verse is to be understood as applying to the sinners who will come out of the Fire. The first view that we mentioned is preferable, namely that the verse's intent is eternity, not limitation.

Al-Wahidi related from al-Hasan that he said: "By Allah, it is nothing but that when one huqb passes, another enters, then another, and so on forever."

The clause ﴿They will not taste therein any coolness or drink, except boiling water and ghassaq﴾ is a resumptive sentence explaining what the previous clause contains: that they will not taste in Hell, or during the ahqab, any coolness that would benefit them from its heat, nor any drink that would benefit them from their thirst, except hamim, which is boiling water, and ghassaq, which is the pus of the people of the Fire.

It may be in the accusative position as a circumstantial state of the pronoun of the tagheen, or an attribute of the ahqab. The exception is disjunct according to those who take bard to mean sleep. It may also be conjunct, from His saying ﴿drink﴾.

Mujahid, al-Suddi, Abu 'Ubayda, al-Kisa'i, al-Fadl ibn Khalid and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi said: the bard mentioned in this verse is sleep, and from it is the saying of al-Kindi:

*Her cheeks grew cool upon me, so the cold kept me*
*away from her and from kissing her, the cold.*

That is, sleep.

Al-Zajjaj said: that is, they will not taste therein the coolness of wind, nor shade, nor sleep, so bard is made to include these matters.

Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Ibn Zayd said: bardan means rawh (comfort) and rawahah (relief).

The majority read ghassaqan with light pronunciation. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with the doubled sin. Its explanation and the explanation of hamim, and the difference of readings concerning them, have already been mentioned in Surah Sad.

﴿A fitting recompense.﴾ That is, in accordance with their deeds. Jaza' is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and wifaqan is its attribute.

Al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: we recompensed them with a recompense that matched their deeds. Al-Zajjaj said: they were recompensed with a recompense that matched their deeds.

Al-Farra' said: al-wifaq is the plural of al-wafq, and al-wafq and al-muwafiq are one.

Muqatil said: the punishment matched the sin; there is no sin greater than evil, and no punishment greater than the Fire.

Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: their deeds were evil, so Allah brought them what would hurt them.

﴿Indeed, they did not expect a reckoning.﴾ That is, they did not expect the reward of a reckoning.

Al-Zajjaj said: they did not believe in the resurrection, so they did not hope for their reckoning. The clause is a justification for their deserving the mentioned recompense.

﴿And they denied Our signs with vehement denial.﴾ That is, they denied the Quranic verses, or they denied what is more general than them, with intense denial. Fi'ial is from the verbal nouns of the tafa''ul form.

Al-Farra' said: it is an eloquent Yemeni dialect; one says kadhdhabtu kidhdhaban and kharraqtu al-qamis kharraqan.

Al-Jawhari said in al-Sihah: "and they denied Our signs with kidhdhaban" is one of the verbal nouns of the doubled form, because its verbal noun may come as taf'il like al-takleem, as fi'al like kidhdhab, as taf'ilah like tawsiyah, and as mufa''al like "And We tore them to shreds, every shred" [Saba: 19]. The majority read kidhdhaban with doubling.

Ali ibn Abi Talib read it with light pronunciation.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the light and the doubled forms are both the verbal noun of al-mukadhabah (denial).

Ibn 'Umar read kuddhaban with a damma on the kaf and doubling, as the plural of kadhib.

Abu Hatim said: its accusative is circumstantial.

Al-Zamakhshari said: it may also (meaning in this reading) mean the one who is eloquent in lying, as you say rajulun kaddhab like your saying hassan and bakhhal.

﴿And everything We have enumerated in a record.﴾ The majority read wa-kulla with the accusative by the construction of suppression: that is, "And We have enumerated everything We have enumerated."

Abu al-Simak read it with the nominative as an inceptive, and what follows is its predicate, and this clause is interposed between the cause and its effect. The accusative of kitaban is a verbal noun for ahsaynahu, since ahsaynahu has the meaning of kataba-nahu (We wrote it). It is also said it is accusative as a circumstantial state: that is, written. It is said the meaning is what We wrote in the Preserved Tablet so that the angels would know it. It is said it means what the guardian angels wrote concerning the deeds of the servants. It is also said it means knowledge, since what is written is further from being forgotten. The first is preferable, given His saying: ﴿And everything We have enumerated in a clear record﴾ [Ya-Sin: 12].

﴿So taste, for We will not increase you except in punishment.﴾ This clause is causally linked to their disbelief and denial of the signs.

Al-Razi said: this fa' is for the recompense, indicating that the command to taste is grounded in the previously explained evil of their deeds. Among the increase in their punishment is that whenever their skins are burned, Allah replaces them with other skins, and whenever the fire subsides, Allah increases them in blaze.

Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿about the great news﴾ that he said: it is the Quran. This is also narrated from a group of the Successors.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying ﴿and We made a blazing lamp﴾ that he said: shining. ﴿And We sent down from the rain-clouds﴾ he said: the clouds. ﴿Water pouring forth﴾ he said: poured out.

Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Ya'la, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning ﴿pouring forth﴾ that he said: poured out.

Al-Shafi'i, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning His saying ﴿And We sent down from the rain-clouds water pouring forth﴾ that he said: Allah sends the wind, and it carries the water, and the clouds pass over it and are milked like a milch camel is milked. The pouring water descends from the sky like great drops, and the winds scatter it so that it falls in scattered form.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Anbari in al-Masahif related from Qatadah that he said: in the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, "And We sent down from the rain-clouds by the winds."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying ﴿And gardens of thick foliage﴾ that he said: intertwined.

Ibn Jarir also related from him concerning the verse that he said: he says: some of it has entwined with others.

Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him concerning His saying ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion and will become a mirage﴾ that he said: the mirage of the sun, which is the shimmering.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him (Ibn Abbas) regarding ﴿lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾ (﴿remaining therein for ages﴾) that he said: "Years."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Hannad, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Salim ibn Abi al-Jaʿd, who said: ʿAli ibn Abi Talib asked Hilal al-Hajari: "What do you find the ḥuqb (an extremely long, indefinite span of time) to be in the Book of Allah?" He replied: "We find it to be eighty years, each year consisting of twelve months, each month thirty days, and each day a thousand years."

Saʿid ibn Mansur and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Masʿud regarding the verse that he said: "One ḥuqb is eighty years."

al-Bazzar narrated from Abu Hurayra, traced back to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, a year is three hundred and sixty days, and a day is like a thousand years of what you count."

ʿAbd ibn Humayd narrated from him (Abu Hurayra) that he said: "The ḥuqb is eighty years, a day of which is like a sixth of the world."

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated...

al-Suyuti said: With a weak chain, from Abu Umama, from the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding ﴿lābithīna fīhā aḥqābā﴾, he said: "The ḥuqb is a thousand months, a month is thirty days, and a year is twelve months, three hundred and sixty days, each day of which is a thousand years of what you count. So the ḥuqb is thirty thousand years."

al-Bazzar, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "By Allah, whoever enters the Fire will not leave it until he remains in it for ages. The ḥuqb is some eighty years, each year is three hundred and sixty days, and each day is a thousand years of what you count."

Ibn Umar said: "So let no one rely on the belief that he will leave the Fire."
